query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature simultaneous wear and corrosion conditions, the intrinsically heterogeneous lamellar structure of eutectic high‐entropy alloys accelerates degradation because friction‐induced heating forms a thermally grown oxide film that is compositionally and mechanically inhomogeneous. Differential oxidation between the dissimilar phase regions (which act as anodic and cathodic sites) induces localized galvanic coupling. Cyclic mechanical loads then spall the fragile, poorly adherent oxide, exposing fresh, active areas that preferentially corrode and rapidly wear. This feedback loop of oxide formation, spallation, and localized corrosion explains the accelerated coupled degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high‐entropy alloy exhibiting a fine dual-phase lamellar microstructure (e.g., alternating Al–Ni–rich and Fe–Cr–rich regions corresponding to FCC/BCC or FCC/B2 phases) that is inherently galvanically heterogeneous.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to cyclic sliding wear at elevated temperatures (600–900 °C) in a corrosive environment (e.g., containing chloride ions), where both frictional heating and corrosive attack occur simultaneously.
generation.conditions: Elevated test temperatures (600–900 °C), a corrosive medium with aggressive ions (e.g., NaCl-containing solutions or atmospheres), and repeated sliding contact that promotes frictional heating and mechanical removal of surface layers.
generation.structural_mediator: The eutectic lamellar microstructure creates distinct phase boundaries with different chemical compositions that develop uneven, galvanically active oxide layers; these inhomogeneities mediate the localized spallation and pitting.
generation.mechanism: Frictional heating at elevated temperature leads to rapid oxidation; however, due to the differential composition inherent in the eutectic structure, the protective oxide film is nonuniform. Mechanical stresses from sliding cause preferential spallation of the poorly adherent, oxide-rich regions. This exposes fresh anodic regions that, because of galvanic coupling between the phases, corrode more rapidly. The mutually reinforcing processes of wear-induced oxide removal and galvanically driven pitting result in accelerated total degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a carefully matched homogenized single-phase alloy baseline, the eutectic multiphase alloy will show significantly higher overall degradation. Specifically, the wear rate (e.g., wear volume) will be increased due to oxide spallation, and the corrosion rate (e.g., pitting density and anodic dissolution) will be enhanced due to local galvanic effects. The combination of these effects will lead to a markedly higher total material loss under identical testing conditions.
generation.baseline: A chemically and microstructurally homogenized high‐entropy alloy with similar bulk composition but a single-phase structure that minimizes galvanic coupling and develops a more uniform, adherent oxide film under the same wear-corrosion conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies when the testing is conducted under high-temperature conditions (600–900 °C) where frictional heating is sufficient to form and destabilize oxide layers, in environments containing corrosive species (e.g., chloride ions), and in materials where the eutectic lamellar spacing is on a scale that fosters galvanic interactions.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence indicates that oxide film formation under friction (PMC12156342::web::036, PMC7515071::web::013) and galvanic effects in multiphase eutectic alloys (PMC12735082::web::000, PMC9319277::web::013) each independently contribute to degradation, the exact quantitative interplay of these two effects under combined wear–corrosion conditions remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of specimens: (1) a eutectic high-entropy alloy retaining its natural dual-phase lamellar microstructure, and (2) a homogenized, single-phase version of the same alloy (achieved through post-processing that suppresses phase segregation). Subject both series to identical cyclic sliding wear tests at 600–900 °C in a controlled corrosive environment (e.g., with a chloride-containing electrolyte or atmosphere).
measurements: Total wear volume and wear track depth (using laser scanning microscopy/SEM)
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., corrosion current density, impedance spectra) to assess pitting and uniform corrosion rates
Characterization of the surface oxide film (using XRD and SEM/EDS) to evaluate thickness, adherence, and spallation extent
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the eutectic multiphase alloy does not exhibit significantly higher total degradation—meaning no statistically meaningful increase in wear volume, oxide spallation, and localized pitting corrosion—compared to the single-phase homogenized composition under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis linking microstructural heterogeneity with the accelerated coupled degradation is falsified.
